title: The political fight over nuclear is distracting from solving price and emissions problems now
oneLiner: Attention and capital spent on a 2040s technology are not spent on the 2020s transition.
body: Policy attention is finite. A multi-year argument about reactors that could not run for fifteen years crowds out decisions on transmission, storage, gas firming and household electrification that determine bills and emissions this decade. On this view the debate is costly even if repeal itself is harmless.
contextBackground: This argument is about the debate rather than the law. It is made by people who might accept repeal in principle but regard the current contest as a delaying tactic, and by energy-industry voices who want policy certainty for projects already under way.
contextDisagreement: Opponents of this claim say it proves too much: any long-horizon decision could be called a distraction. They also note that a legislated ban is itself a political choice that forecloses the long horizon.

otherClaim.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation

claimItself.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
claimItself.body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.
